Les diplômés du Collège de Sainte-Anne e: Graduates of Collège de Sainte-Anne and Queen of Angels Academy felt a chill run down their spines last week.
<strong>Un héritage à Lachine qui s’éten: A Legacy in Lachine That Keeps Growing
En 1861, les Sœurs de Sainte-Anne ont fo: In 1861, the Sisters of Saint Anne founded Collège Sainte-Anne in Lachine, a francophone institution that now offers elementary, secondary and college-level education. Collège de Sainte-Anne also operates an elementary school and a high school on the former site of Queen Of Angels school, in Dorval.
Elise Legault, qui a obtenu son diplôme: Elise Legault, who graduated from the Lachine high school in 2007, reacted strongly when she learned that the founding Sisters had been present in the residential schools. It was La Converse’s investigation that informed her. She has since written a letter to the principal of her former high school, Ugo Cavenaghi. “Your prestigious college is an ostentatious display of the legacy of the Sisters of Saint Anne congregation. Your vision draws on it. The relentless expansion of your enterprise and your deployment of student ambassadors internationally bear the mark of the missionary. You proudly show off the history of the Sisters of Saint Anne, which you call a ‘Grand Legacy.’ Am I therefore wrong to expect a reaction from Collège Sainte-Anne?” she writes in the letter she sent us. To date, the principal has not answered her questions. Ms. Legault denounces the nuns’ “murderous mission,” carried out across the country. “I went to Collège Sainte-Anne in Lachine, I wore that crest,” she says vehemently.
La professionnelle en communications n’a: The communications professional doesn’t recall residential schools ever being mentioned in her history classes. By the time she attended high school, the Sisters of Saint Anne had left the school’s administration.
Malgré la proximité de la maison-mère et: Despite the proximity of the adjoining motherhouse and convent, they were no longer involved in school life, and Ms. Legault was unaware of their missions. “The place was still steeped in religion. The legacy of the Sisters of Saint Anne was very ostentatious there,” she recalls. Ms. Legault, who is not kind toward the Sisters’ legacy, also laments that the school’s administration refuses to speak out when its name signals its belonging to the congregation. She believes the institution wants to protect its image at all costs.
« Ils aiment l’attention et se faire cél: “They like attention and being celebrated. But they need to act according to the values they claim to hold. The administration should use its powers and its privilege to ask questions and demand accountability from the congregation,” says the former student, who sent her request to the administration in writing. She also wants the Sisters of Saint Anne to be held accountable. “I want their full cooperation in making the archives available to Indigenous nations, who will then decide what they want to do with them.” She points to the agreement stipulating that these archives remain under the nuns’ custody until 2027. “Considering the context, that seems disrespectful to me.”
Le 3 juin dernier, nous nous sommes prés: On June 3, we went to Collège de Saint-Anne in Lachine. The site is reminiscent of the Sisters of Saint Anne’s motherhouse, not far away. The administration did not want to meet with us and invited us to contact the communications department by email. We emailed several staff members repeatedly. As of this writing, our emails have gone unanswered.
Les élèves de l’école secondaire Queen o: Students of Queen of Angels Academy (QAA), the high school founded in 1888 by the Sisters of Saint Anne in Dorval, are also seeking answers from the nuns. “I fell off my chair,” exclaims Catherine Doyle, who graduated from the girls’ high school in 1989, describing the moment she learned that the nuns who taught her were linked to the remains of 215 Indigenous children found at the Kamloops residential school.
C’est un gazouillis du First Nations Lea: She found out through a tweet from the First Nations Leadership Council calling on the premier to make public the Catholic Church archives held by the province of British Columbia. “The Sisters of Saint Anne taught generations of young women at Queen of Angels,” she says. Ms. Doyle, who was taught by nuns, had never known that the Sisters were tied to Indigenous residential schools. “We all knew that the congregation was devoted to education.
On nous a enseigné l’histoire de la fond: We were taught the story of the founder and of the schools the Sisters created in Montréal,” she tells us over the phone. According to her, the subject of residential schools was never addressed. Together with a classmate, Amy McLean, Ms. Doyle informed a group of alumnae of her discovery. Reactions were strong. The same goes for students who attended the anglophone private school in Dorval more recently, before it closed its doors in 2014. Nuns lived on campus.
Après avoir lu <l1>l’enquête de La Conve: After reading <l1>La Converse’s investigation,</l1> Ms. Doyle wanted to hold the congregation to account. Several former students have also sent letters to the Sisters of Saint Anne in British Columbia and in Lachine. The former students issued a call to action asking the Sisters to disclose their records and archives. “We also believe they must acknowledge the facts and apologize for their involvement. And we think it’s important not to stop at an apology, but that there must be action tied to the apology. They must take steps and make amends for their role in the suffering, the harm and the cultural devastation they caused through the residential schools,” says Ms. Doyle, who admits to being disappointed by the congregation’s lack of transparency.
Hayley Morris, ancienne élève de Queen O: Hayley Morris, a former Queen of Angels Academy student, in front of St. Francis Xavier Church in Kahnawá:ke, and the shoes left in commemoration by members of her community. Photo: courtesy of Hayley Morris
Comme de nombreuses femmes et filles de: Like many women and girls from her community, Megan Kanerahtenha:wi Whyte, an artist and Indigenous art therapy teacher, attended Queen of Angels Academy, where she graduated from high school in 2007. She followed in the footsteps of her mother, who had attended the school a generation earlier. Every day, a school bus took her and her classmates from Kahnawá:ke to Dorval.
« À l’époque, les frais de scolarité éta: “Back then, tuition was very affordable, because the Sisters wanted to make education accessible to everyone, regardless of social class,” she recalls. It was through a post by Christine Boyle in an online group for the school’s graduates that Ms. Kanerahtenha:wi Whyte learned of the Sisters of Saint Anne’s involvement in the residential schools. After the initial shock, she went through a whole range of emotions. “It was a surprise, but also not a surprise,” she says, explaining how the history of residential schools is inextricable from that of her family and her community.
« La surprise était qu’il s’agissait de: “The surprise was that it was the school I attended. But it wasn’t so surprising, because it was run by nuns,” says the woman, who took time to digest the news. She is still reflecting on it, raising the notion of intergenerational trauma. “These are things we heard about growing up. It’s the disappointment, the anger and the wounds it reopens,” she says, speaking of the discovery of the 215 bodies in Kamloops. Even though the residential schools are no longer in operation, for the artist this is a living history, one with a lasting impact on Indigenous communities and families, then and now.
Plusieurs membres de sa famille ont fréq: Several members of her family attended Indigenous day schools, those compulsory schools where students were not boarders. Her grandfather is a residential school survivor. “Before, he and his family spoke the language fluently. In my father’s generation and in mine, we don’t have access to the language,” the artist says with emotion. “That’s a direct effect of residential schools on my own family. When I was young, and then as a parent, I fought very hard to learn my language and to make sure my daughter knew her language.
Ce sont les choses auxquelles je réfléch: Those are the things I’ve been thinking about since I heard the news about the Sisters of Saint Anne: all the ways residential schools are implicated in my family and my community, knowing how it affects me, how it affects my family and my children. It’s a lot,” she tells us. She remembers her time in high school. “They mentioned that the Algonquins and the Iroquois existed. In five years of education, only a few minutes were devoted to Indigenous history,” she says of her history classes.
« Quand j’étais jeune, ça m’a semblé trè: “When I was young, it felt like I wasn’t valued at all. Like I wasn’t a real person.” Hayley Morris attended Queen of Angels Academy for the first two years of high school, before finishing her studies at a different private high school in 2014. The accounting student rode the bus from the Kahnawá:ke reserve with her classmates. “It breaks my heart to find out that a school I attended was associated with something like this,” says the young woman.
« J’y ai passé un bon moment, j’y ai été: “I had a good time there, I was really made to feel welcome, like all the Indigenous students who were enrolled,” recalls Ms. Morris. “It’s hard. It makes me sad and angry,” she says, after learning the news in the media last Friday.
L’étudiante, qui travaille au Mohawk Cou: The student, who works in the finance department at the Mohawk Council, wants the Sisters of Saint Anne to acknowledge their responsibility. “For me, the first step toward reconciliation is acknowledgement. If you don’t do that, it’s a real slap in the face,” she believes.
« Reconnaître le fait que ces atrocités: “Acknowledging that these atrocities took place in governments and in the Church, writing history books and talking about it”: that is what Ms. Morris proposes as a first step toward reconciliation. While she says it may be a buzzword, the young woman nonetheless hopes that, through these conversations, everyone will then ask themselves: “What can we do about this?” Ms. Kanerahtenha:wi Whyte addresses the subject of reconciliation extensively through art therapy and community art, as well as the notions of <l1>cultural safety</l1> and intergenerational trauma.
« Les pensionnats étaient destinés à cré: “Residential schools were designed to create a rupture, in every way imaginable. How do we rebuild the bridges that were cut, together? How can we build relationships together while knowing where we come from?” she asks. Repairing a relationship is how the artist describes reconciliation, a term about which she has mixed feelings. “It implies that there was a relationship to begin with,” she points out. “If you think about it, there has never been a healthy relationship with Indigenous peoples since the onslaught of colonization. And there still isn’t.” To arrive at the healthy relationship we want, it has to be built on listening, empathy and meeting people where they are, believes the art therapy teacher.
« C’est la base. Il faut se voir », obse: “That’s the foundation. We have to see each other,” she observes. For Megan Kanerahtenha:wi Whyte and Hayley Morris, it is also crucial to dismantle stereotypes and understand intergenerational trauma. “I feel like people need to understand what happened in history so that it gets passed down in families. People need to understand what Indigenous people have lived through and continue to live through, in order to shed light on the forms of colonization and systemic violence that persist today,” says Kanerahtenha:wi Whyte, who wants these issues to be addressed in political discussions as well.
« On commence avec les pensionnats, mais: “We’re starting with residential schools, but there are societal problems that stem from the horrible things people have lived through, including trauma and alcoholism,” she adds. “If people understood where it comes from, they would be less ignorant,” she believes. Students of Little Flower Academy, the girls’ high school founded by the Sisters of Saint Anne in British Columbia, are also demanding apologies from the religious congregation.
<strong>Mise à jour des Sœurs de Sainte-: Update from the Sisters of Saint Anne
Depuis notre publication du 14 juin dern: Since our June 14 publication, the religious congregation has updated <l1>the home page of its website</l1>. It now includes a section titled “Indian Residential Schools.”
« Il y a quelques années, avec une profo: “A few years ago, with deep sadness and great regret, we realized that some of the teaching positions accepted by the Sisters of Saint Anne in British Columbia were destructive to the children the Sisters had intended to serve. These positions were in four ‘Indian Industrial Residential Schools.’ Kamloops was one of them,” it reads. The congregation adds that it regrets having contributed to them.
Depuis le 21 juin dernier, les Soeurs de: Since June 21, the Sisters of Saint Anne have signed <l1>a new agreement </l1>with the Royal BC Museum regarding access to their archives. The agreement provides for better dialogue with the National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation and the Residential School History and Dialogue Centre.
